Lessons.Title: Data Representations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: draw and interpret a dot plot, histogram and box plot for the same numerical dataset; calculate a five-number summary; and explain the effect of changing histogram bins. Optional review lesson in Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition, Unit 1 Lesson 2 (CC BY 4.0), https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/2/preparation.html. The source lists 6.SP.B.4 as Building On, HSS-ID.A.1 as Addressing and HSS-ID.A.2 as Building Towards.

Edulytiks original practice dataset (12 recorded cycling-trip durations, minutes): 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10. All values are nonnegative numerical measurements. A dot plot displays one dot for each trip at its numerical value. An accessible count description appears in the accompanying frequency table.

A histogram groups numerical observations into nonoverlapping intervals. For bins [2,4), [4,6), [6,8), [8,10), [10,12), the frequencies are 3, 3, 3, 2, 1. Left endpoints are included; right endpoints are excluded, so 4 belongs to [4,6), not [2,4). Axes must be titled 'Trip duration (minutes)' and 'Number of trips', with bars touching because time is numerical.

Rebinning the same data into [2,6), [6,10), [10,14) yields frequencies 6, 5, 1. The sum is still 12, but the visual impression changes. Choose intervals appropriate to the data and disclose their boundaries; do not infer a different sample from a re-binned graph.

For the box plot, first sort the values. With 12 observations, the median is the average of positions 6 and 7: (5+6)/2 = 5.5. The lower six are 2,3,3,4,5,5; Q1 = (3+4)/2 = 3.5. The upper six are 6,7,7,8,9,10; Q3 = (7+8)/2 = 7.5. The minimum is 2 and maximum is 10. On a minutes number line, draw a box from 3.5 to 7.5, a median mark at 5.5, and whiskers to 2 and 10. This uses the median-of-halves convention; state your quartile convention for larger datasets.

Student tasks: (1) create a dot plot of all twelve measurements and identify its mode(s); (2) draw both histograms, specifying boundaries and labels, and explain how their appearances differ; (3) calculate the summary and draw the matching box plot; (4) compare what individual values a dot plot preserves versus what each grouped display hides. Teacher rubric: 0–2 points each for accurate dot counts, histograms and axis/interval labels, correct five-number calculation and box positions, and a reasoned graphical comparison. Maximum 8; 0 missing/incorrect, 1 partially correct, 2 complete and justified. Original drawing and reasoning require human review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dot plot
KeyConcepts.Definition: One mark is placed over each recorded numerical value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count all marks; equal values stack at the same horizontal position.
KeyConcepts.Example: For value 3, place two dots at 3 minutes; for 7, two dots at 7 minutes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Histogram bin
KeyConcepts.Definition: A continuous numerical interval grouping observations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For [a,b), include a and exclude b; adjoining intervals must not overlap or leave gaps.

KeyConcepts.Title: Five-number summary
KeyConcepts.Definition: Minimum, lower quartile Q1, median Q2, upper quartile Q3 and maximum.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Sort the data, calculate each statistic using a declared quartile method and keep its units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Box plot
KeyConcepts.Definition: A display of five-number summary and the spread of the data.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Draw median within Q1–Q3 box; extend whiskers to min/max when using this simple convention.
KeyConcepts.Example: The IQR is 7.5−3.5 = 4 minutes, and the full range is 10−2 = 8 minutes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count and bin the trip durations
WorkedExamples.Question: Create a frequency description and histogram counts for 12 trips using intervals [2,4), [4,6), [6,8), [8,10), [10,12).
WorkedExamples.Method: Tally each raw observation once according to left-inclusive, right-exclusive interval boundaries.
Steps: Read 2,3,3: three observations are at least 2 and less than 4.
Read 4,5,5: three observations are at least 4 and less than 6.
Read 6,7,7: three observations are at least 6 and less than 8.
Read 8,9: two observations are at least 8 and less than 10.
Read 10: one observation is at least 10 and less than 12.
Check frequencies 3+3+3+2+1 = 12, matching all raw observations.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The five bar heights are 3,3,3,2,1; bins have width 2 minutes.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every one of the 12 trip durations appears in exactly one interval and the total frequency is 12.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute a five-number summary
WorkedExamples.Question: For the same sorted 12 durations, find min, Q1, median, Q3, max and interpret the interquartile range.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the median-of-halves quartile definition, then subtract Q1 from Q3.
Steps: The minimum is the first value 2, and maximum is the last value 10.
Median is mean of positions 6 and 7: (5+6)/2 = 5.5.
WorkedExamples.Check: The statistics are ordered 2 ≤ 3.5 ≤ 5.5 ≤ 7.5 ≤ 10, and half the data fall within the central quartile interval by construction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rebin a histogram without changing the data
WorkedExamples.Question: Give frequencies for [2,6), [6,10), [10,14) using the same 12 trip durations.
WorkedExamples.Method: Place each numerical observation in one left-inclusive interval.
Steps: Add frequencies 6 + 5 + 1 = 12, matching the original sample.
WorkedExamples.Check: All 12 observations appear exactly once; no boundary value is counted twice.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting a boundary value in two histogram bins.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Double counting inflates total frequency and changes the represented data.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a consistent [lower, upper) bin convention; a 6-minute trip belongs only to [6,8).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the median and quartiles as individual data values without computing when the sample size is even.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The central statistic may lie between observed values.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Order observations and average the two middle values of the relevant group.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a histogram shows individual data points precisely.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the dot plot for exact values and label the histogram bins and counts explicitly.

SummaryPoints: For the 12-trip dataset, dot-plot frequencies are 2:1,3:2,4:1,5:2,6:1,7:2,8:1,9:1,10:1.
Width-two histogram bin frequencies: 3,3,3,2,1; width-four frequencies: 6,5,1; both total 12.
Five-number summary is (2,3.5,5.5,7.5,10) minutes under the median-of-halves convention.
Class-created dot plots, box plots, histogram choices and explanations require teacher rubric assessment; single numeric answers do not replace these tasks.

Visuals.Title: Accessible dot plot counts for the same 12 cycling trips
Visuals.Description: Frequency table specifies every point of an independently authored dot plot: each dot represents one trip; durations and counts are provided for nonvisual interpretation.

Visuals.Title: Histogram bins at width 2 minutes
Visuals.Description: Continuous intervals are left-inclusive and right-exclusive; horizontal axis is duration in minutes, vertical axis is the number of trips.
